title: Probing Surface Vibrational Modes in Catalytic Nanoparticles by Electron Energy-Loss Spectroscopy
content: The vibrational modes associated with surfaces may play critical roles in processes such as chemical conversions and energy transfer. For example, in a thermochemical reaction, electron transfer takes place between components to bring about a chemical transformation. Before electron transfer can occur, electrons are thermally excited to higher energy states via transitions between vibrational energy levels. The rate of electron transfer can be greatly accelerated through the use of heterogeneous catalysts which lowers the activation energy at active sites on the catalyst surface. The catalyst is often in the form of nanoparticles and the active sites are highly localized at the atomic level. The role of surface vibrations and phonons for such a process is not clear in part because of the absence of local experimental measurements. There are three types of vibrational modes that may be present on a catalyst surface. First there may be phonon modes localized on surfaces layers, e.g. surface phonons such as Rayleigh modes, and distinct vibrational modes at surface defects. Second, there are more delocalized surface phonon polaritons (e.g. Fuchs-Kliewer modes) which may also be excited by IR radiation associated with heat. Third, during catalysis, adsorbate species are present on the catalyst surface giving rise to molecular vibrational modes. These molecular modes may couple with the other modes at nanoparticle surfaces. We are interested in locally exploring these diverse vibrational phenomena associated with catalytic nanoparticle surfaces using vibrational electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) in a scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM) [1].
